**The short version.** *Each line links to where it is argued below.*

- **One direction only.** ICD-10-CM names failure in extraordinary detail. [Ask what right looks like](#the-asymmetry) and the vocabulary runs out.
- **Measures of health do exist.** EQ-5D, SF-36, PROMIS, HALE, Life's Essential 8, intrinsic capacity, fitness percentiles. [Every one](#what-we-built-instead) subtracts deficit from a ceiling, covers one domain, or describes populations rather than people.
- **A metric is an agreement.** It records what a society decided to care about, exactly enough for strangers to act together. [Leave something unstandardised](#what-a-metric-is-for) and whoever is loudest defines it.
- **Thresholds are cheap; gradients are unclaimed.** Two 30-year-olds at 118/76 and 105/65 clear the same bar, and nothing we have agreed on can rank them. Most of us live up there.
- **What any answer needs:** [a definition two analysts could run and match](#what-it-would-take-to-start-closing-it), spread shown rather than hidden, value on its own terms, and a funder who wants it settled.

None of this gets closed by FRESH. It works inside the gap, treating disagreement between food scoring systems as evidence.

That gap runs downstream too, into who can ever be told to stop: [Part 2](../we-measure-harm-we-mean-benefit/).
:::

There are 74,719 codes in ICD-10-CM as of last October,[^icd] the vocabulary US clinicians use to name what is wrong with you: severe sepsis with septic shock (R65.21), frostbite of an unspecified ear (T33.019A), an ingrown nail (L60.0). Every lab value, every guideline, every billable encounter turns *is this person sick?* into a binary somebody can act on.

Ask that same apparatus whether you are healthy and the answers come back made of one material. Healthy means no diagnosis. Healthy means low predicted risk. Healthy means years of life not lost to illness. There is no agreed metric of health defined by anything other than the subtraction of disease.[^revision]

That subtraction hides behind language that sounds positive. The CDC defines health equity as "the state in which everyone has a fair and just opportunity to attain their highest level of health." Highest level of *what*, measured how? The sentence presumes a measurement we do not have.

I have been asking about that missing measurement in public for two years, in various ways. March was the bluntest.

> "We have TONS of ways to tell if you're diseased. You've probably already been told that. But health? That piece is still elusive. Why?"

That question keeps going unanswered. Here is my attempt at why.

## What a metric is for

Part of the answer sits in what a metric is: an agreement rather than a discovery, stating what a society decided to care about precisely enough that strangers can act on it together. Those 74,719 codes are an accumulated decision about what deserves naming, tracking, paying for and fighting over. Somebody sat on a committee and concluded that a frostbitten ear of unrecorded side earns its own entry, and that judgment is now infrastructure shaping what well over a million US clinicians can see.

Which makes the missing health metric a missing agreement rather than a missing number. Nobody has said out loud which health we want, in terms specific enough to be held to. People have argued the definition for decades: the WHO wrote one into its constitution in 1948, and a literature has pushed back ever since.[^define] What that argument never produced is a quantity a clinician, a payer or a shopper could act on.

Producing one would not require a perfect instrument, and could not deliver one: measurement compresses something complicated into something comparable, and the compression always loses. Comparability is the point: a standard lets a clinician in Ohio and a regulator in Brussels find out that they disagree, and about what. Meanwhile what goes unstandardised goes to whoever is most confident. Wellness marketing means whatever the seller needs this quarter, and four people at one table hold four ideas about a good diet, none of them checkable.

But the strongest objection is real: health is too rich and too personal to compress into a number. That objection is correct, and it settles which metric rather than whether. A rich thing measured roughly can still be audited and revised by people who were not in the room. A rich thing left unmeasured goes to the loudest voice.

## The asymmetry

Confidence is what the disease side has never lacked. We have built an enormous measurement literature for what goes wrong, and most of it sits unused. The Tufts registry holds 1,382 cardiovascular prediction models, 58% of them never externally validated even once.[^cvd] Framingham, QRISK, SCORE2, the Pooled Cohort Equations, PREVENT: most clinicians can name one or two, and the rest stay on shelves, accumulating in the thousands for more than 25 years now.[^shelves]

PREVENT is the newest, published in 2023 and installed in the 2025 ACC/AHA blood pressure guideline in place of the Pooled Cohort Equations. It roughly halves estimated ten-year risk, from a mean of 9.0% to 4.6%, moving about half of US adults into a lower risk category.[^prevent1] Any of these inverts: a 5% ten-year risk is a 95% chance of no event, which you are welcome to call your cardiovascular health. The inversion is arithmetically fine and philosophically empty. A probability of avoiding one event inside one window is not vitality, not reserve, not resilience. Press on the word *health* anywhere in this literature and it collapses into absence of disease.

Absence of disease is necessary, which is worth conceding, because it is the best objection to the essay. Disease infrastructure tells you when you have crossed a line that means something has broken. What it never measures is the range above the line. A 30-year-old at 118/76 and a 30-year-old at 105/65 are both not hypertensive, and we have no way of saying whether they are equally healthy. The same holds for HRV, VO2 max, lipids, fasting glucose, sleep architecture, every variable where disease has a threshold and health has a gradient.

That gradient is where the near-misses live. Biological age clocks aim at the positive pole, and the question behind them is legitimate: how old does this body look from the inside? The first clocks were trained to predict chronological age, the later ones against mortality and disease.[^clocks] What reaches consumers is positive framing wrapped around a deficit model. Food scoring fails from the other side: more than 200 published systems exist, and five of them scored one loaf of whole wheat bread from the 12th to the 99th percentile.[^bread]

Those systems are all chasing a term the federal guidelines use without operationalising. The Dietary Guidelines do define nutrient-dense foods, as foods that "provide vitamins, minerals, and other health-promoting components and have no or limited added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium."[^dga] That is a sentence, and you cannot compute it. Two analysts holding the same composition table and the same words will not return the same number, which is how a field ends up with 200 systems, and how health equity, the production of health and every other second-order claim comes to rest on a first-order quantity nobody has agreed how to compute.

## What we built instead

Nobody agreed how to compute it, though not for want of trying, and naming what does exist makes the gap sharper rather than smaller. Start with the case that comes closest to refuting me. In 2022 the American Heart Association published Life's Essential 8, a 0-to-100 cardiovascular health score for an individual: diet, physical activity, nicotine exposure, sleep, body mass index, lipids, glucose, blood pressure. Its presidential advisory traces the construct to a deliberate shift toward positive health promotion rather than disease treatment alone.[^le8] Same organisation that produced PREVENT, same domain, a serious attempt. Then look at the assembly: eight familiar risk factors, each scored against cutoffs that exist because they predict events. A behaviour-and-biomarker checklist, scored well, inheriting its scale from what it is trying not to be.

That inheritance repeats outside cardiology. NIH funded PROMIS through the Common Fund to standardise self-reported health, with item banks for Positive Affect, Life Satisfaction, and Meaning and Purpose.[^promis] NICE requires EQ-5D as its reference measure, and EQ-5D asks about mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain and anxiety, scaling down from full health.[^eq5d] SF-36 has been in service since the 1990s. WHO has published healthy life expectancy since 2000, healthspan at population scale, computed by taking years lost to disability off years lived.[^hale] All real, all validated, all in use, and every one puts the ceiling of its scale where nothing is wrong.

Against that ceiling, ageing research has pushed hardest. WHO's intrinsic capacity framework scores five domains, one of them literally vitality, and English general practice runs an electronic frailty index across everyone aged 65 and over.[^icope] VO2 max, which I called a gradient nobody had agreed what to do with, turns out to have percentile norms by age and sex from the FRIEND registry, and an AHA statement argued in 2016 for treating fitness as a clinical vital sign.[^crf] We agreed where you sit in the distribution. We never agreed what sitting there makes you.

Those instruments all lean one way. Two constructs lean the other. Allostatic load points exactly where a positive measure should point, at cumulative physiological wear, and after three decades it has no settled operationalisation: published indices run from six to sixteen biomarkers with no consistent method.[^allostatic] The Global Burden of Disease study, the most careful health accounting on earth, reports disability-adjusted life years, so its unit of health is a unit of health destroyed.[^gbd]

Put that inventory together and my claim survives with one word changed. Every agreed measure is derived from deficit, covers a single domain, or runs at population scale only, and as far as I can find none of them is consulted when a person decides what to eat or whether to keep taking something.

## Why the gap is still open

How it stayed that way I can only guess at. Three guesses follow, and I do not know which is most right.

**One: we built what could be billed.** Disease has a payer, a code and a trial endpoint. Health has none of the three. PROMIS proves NIH will fund an instrument when somebody asks, so patronage exists in patches, but no payer, guideline or product label I know of turns on a positive measure the way nearly everything turns on a diagnosis.

**Two: health may be genuinely harder to measure.** Disease is the perturbation and health is the equilibrium, and we are better at noticing what broke than at describing what holds. That may be a cognitive asymmetry or an artifact of the tradition we inherited. I am not sure.

**Three: the incentives all point at disease.** Publication rewards novel mechanisms, pipelines reward treatments, trials reward endpoints, and even prevention research gets scored by cases averted. A health metric would have to compete against metrics already working for everyone whose funding depends on them.

None of the three gets less true while the gap stays unnamed.

## Naming it

I have been calling it the health gap. The name is clunky and it collides with health-equity gaps, healthspan gaps and the access gap, so better ones are welcome. What a name has to do here is make one asymmetry visible: an enormous apparatus for half of what we say we want, and instruments for the other half that measure the first half backwards. You cannot fix what you cannot point at.

## What it would take to start closing it

Pointing is the cheap part. I have no research program in my back pocket, but I can name the conditions any defensible answer would meet.

**It has to be computable.** A construct with named subcomponents, specified instruments and stated aggregation rules, so that two analysts applying it to one case come back with one number. Imperfect is fine. Vague is not.

**It has to carry its uncertainty in the open.** Health is a one-and-the-many problem before it is an empirical one, so a serious measure shows its spread instead of hiding it under a statistic that implies precision the construct cannot support.

**It has to be worth something on its own terms.** A measure that matters only because it predicts disease incidence is a disease measure wearing a different label, and that is where most wellness measurement collapses.

**It has to be readable by the people it is for.** A coordination device nobody can read coordinates nothing, and this condition gets skipped most. In the 2023 international adult skills survey, 34% of US adults scored at or below Level 1 in numeracy against an OECD average of 25%, and the share at or below Level 1 in literacy went from 19% to 28% in six years.[^piaac] In 2003, at the last national measurement of US health literacy, reading a healthy weight range off a height-and-weight graph scored at Intermediate difficulty, which by my reading of where that task sits puts it beyond roughly half of adults.[^naal] A federal agency put a difficulty score on an artifact the nutrition field hands out for free.

The easy reading of those numbers blames the audience. Look at the professionals and that reflex weakens. Given a screening question in conditional-probability form, 160 gynecologists picked the right answer 21% of the time, worse than guessing among four options; after a training session that taught them to translate those probabilities into natural frequencies, 87% got it right.[^formats] The design cannot separate format from teaching, and I no longer claim it can. It does show that the numbers as normally presented were unusable until somebody stopped and taught the translation.

Teaching that translation is nowhere near routine. In one survey of US primary care physicians, 47% said that finding more cancers in screened populations proves screening saves lives, which it does not.[^wegwarth] Patient education materials in high-impact journals average a grade 11 to 14 reading level, and 2% meet the AMA's own recommendation.[^readability] Whatever metric gets built ships into that, legible to its authors and to almost nobody else.

**It needs a patron who wants the question settled.** NIH funds instruments and disease endpoints. NSF does not see basic science here. Foundations chase legible outcomes, industry wants something sellable, and somebody has to commission the agreement itself.

**And it has to stop pretending we are further along than we are.** Nearly every public conversation about health prediction, biological age and food scoring included, runs ahead of the foundational measurement. Saying so out loud is the cheapest honest move available.

## FRESH is one attempt

Saying it out loud is roughly what FRESH does on the food side. Three years in, it does not close the gap and does not claim to. It reports the spread across rating systems instead of averaging it away, and states plainly that nobody yet knows what *healthy* means at the level of one food. There should be more attempts than mine.

## The closer

More attempts would need more people, and the people are scattered across nutrition, medicine, public health, wellness technology and philosophy of science. Every time I post the question a few more of them write back. If you are one, building a metric, designing a study, writing the critique, or working out what health even means as a measurable thing, I want to hear from you.

Information can be health. Only if we agree what health is.

That agreement starts with values, and values are the part nobody was taught. Our kids are not taught what a value system is, and neither were we. I have bet in public that more than 95% of PhDs in my adjacent fields never took a philosophy course.[^phil] So the measurement gap sits on an educational one, and the scaffolding that would let the conversation happen was never built.

So why are we still not asking the question seriously?

[^revision]: **Correction, 2026-08-06.** This essay published claiming that no agreed metric of health exists at all, that the space above the diagnostic threshold has no agreed instruments, and that the question has never had an institutional patron. All three were too strong. [What we built instead](#what-we-built-instead) now names the counterexamples: Life's Essential 8, PROMIS, EQ-5D, SF-36, HALE, WHO intrinsic capacity, cardiorespiratory fitness percentiles and frailty indices, several of them in routine use. The narrower claim above is the one that survives contact with them. Two smaller corrections came in the same pass. The ninety-percentile-point spread on a loaf of bread came from five scoring systems rather than from the 200-plus in the literature, and a passage dating three of my LinkedIn posts as spread across fourteen months had the arithmetic wrong and has been cut.

[^cvd]: Wessler, Nelson, Park, et al., "External Validations of Cardiovascular Clinical Prediction Models: A Large-Scale Review of the Literature," *Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and Outcomes* 2021;14(8):e007858, DOI [10.1161/CIRCOUTCOMES.121.007858](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCOUTCOMES.121.007858): 2,030 external validations of 1,382 CPMs in the Tufts Predictive Analytics and Comparative Effectiveness registry, with 807 of them (58%) never externally validated. *(Citation upgraded 2026-08-01; this claim originally rested on [my own June 2024 LinkedIn post](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7212122529354637314/), which is not a source.)* Note the denominator. 1,382 covers cardiovascular CPMs of all kinds published through March 2015, so SCORE2 (2021) and PREVENT (2023) are named above as examples of the field rather than as members of that registry. The narrower set of general-population risk models is smaller: [Damen et al., *BMJ* 2016;353:i2416](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.i2416) found 363. "More than a thousand" is right for the field and would be wrong for Framingham-style tools specifically.

[^prevent1]: PREVENT was published as an AHA scientific statement in 2023, in Khan et al., "Development and Validation of the American Heart Association's PREVENT Equations," *Circulation* 2023;148(24):1982–2004, [PMID 37947094](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37947094/), but it displaced the Pooled Cohort Equations in guideline terms only with the [2025 AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/HYPERTENSIONAHA.125.25465). The magnitude is from Diao et al., *JAMA* 2024, [PMID 39073797](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39073797/): mean 10-year ASCVD risk of 4.6% under PREVENT against 9.0% under the PCEs, reclassifying 53.0% of US adults to a lower risk category. **Correction, 2026-08-06:** this essay published saying PREVENT "replaced the Pooled Cohort Equations in 2023 … overnight," which conflated the publication date with the adoption date and was wrong on both the year and the speed.

[^icd]: **Correction, 2026-08-01.** This essay published with 74,260, which is the FY2025 count. "As of last October" means FY2026, effective 1 October 2025, which is 74,719. Both figures are billable-code counts taken from the CMS `icd10cm_order` files for the respective years. The description line said "roughly 70,000," a rounding that had drifted well below the actual number, and now says 74,719.

[^define]: The WHO constitution of 1948 defines health as "a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity," and the argument over that sentence has run ever since. See Huber et al., "How should we define health?", *BMJ* 2011;343:d4163, [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.d4163), which proposes health as the ability to adapt and self-manage, and the Boorse and Nordenfelt exchange in philosophy of medicine behind it. The conversation did happen, repeatedly. What it has not produced is an operational definition anyone could be held to.

[^shelves]: From January 2025: <https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7281331846217437184/>. The full line: *"We've had risk tools for >25 years. They're accumulating on the shelves in the thousands. Why? My bet (other than incentives) is education."*

[^clocks]: The first epigenetic clocks were trained to predict chronological age: Horvath, "DNA methylation age of human tissues and cell types," *Genome Biology* 2013;14:R115, and Hannum et al., "Genome-wide methylation profiles reveal quantitative views of human aging rates," *Molecular Cell* 2013;49(2):359–367. Later generations were trained against mortality and disease outcomes, which is the version the consumer market sells as biological age. My complaint is about that translation rather than about the research.

[^bread]: [Five verdicts on one loaf](../meta-nps-five-verdicts/): five published nutrient-profiling systems scored the same whole wheat bread from the 12th to the 99th percentile, a spread of 87 points. Those five are a convenience sample of the 200-plus systems in the literature, so the spread demonstrates that the systems disagree and does not estimate the full range across all of them. **Correction, 2026-08-06:** this essay published attributing a ninety-percentile-point spread to the 200-plus population in three separate places.

[^dga]: *Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025*, <https://www.dietaryguidelines.gov/>. Nutrient-dense foods are defined there as foods that "provide vitamins, minerals, and other health-promoting components and have no or limited added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium." So a verbal definition exists. What does not exist is an operational one: no thresholds, no reference amount, no aggregation rule, which is the room in which 200-plus competing scoring systems fit.

[^le8]: Lloyd-Jones et al., "Life's Essential 8: Updating and Enhancing the American Heart Association's Construct of Cardiovascular Health: A Presidential Advisory From the American Heart Association," *Circulation* 2022;146(5):e18–e43, [PMID 35766027](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35766027/). Eight components, each scored 0 to 100 and averaged, with the advisory tracing the construct to the AHA's 2010 move toward positive health promotion and preservation rather than disease treatment alone. I treat it as the strongest counterexample to my own argument, because it is one.

[^promis]: [PROMIS](https://commonfund.nih.gov/promis) was funded through the NIH Common Fund to standardise self-reported health measurement. Alongside the pain, fatigue and physical-function banks it includes Positive Affect, Life Satisfaction, and Meaning and Purpose; on the last of those, see "Assessing meaning & purpose in life: development and validation of an item bank and short forms for the NIH PROMIS," *Quality of Life Research* 2020, [PMID 32306302](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32306302/).

[^eq5d]: NICE, *Health technology evaluations: the manual*, [chapter 4](https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2): EQ-5D is the preferred measure of health-related quality of life in adults, and using anything else counts as a departure from the reference case. Its five dimensions are mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain or discomfort, and anxiety or depression, each scaling down from full health.

[^hale]: WHO, [Healthy life expectancy (HALE)](https://www.who.int/data/gho/indicator-metadata-registry/imr-details/7752), first reported for 191 member states in the *World Health Report 2000* and published through the Global Health Observatory since. HALE is life expectancy adjusted for time lived in states short of full health, so it is built by subtraction and it describes populations rather than people.

[^icope]: WHO's [Integrated Care for Older People](https://www.who.int/teams/maternal-newborn-child-adolescent-health-and-ageing/ageing-and-health/integrated-care-for-older-people-icope) treats intrinsic capacity as five domains, locomotion, vitality, cognition, psychological capacity and sensory function, with a screening tool and a care pathway attached. In England, [routine frailty identification](https://www.england.nhs.uk/ourwork/clinical-policy/older-people/frailty/efi/) for patients aged 65 and over entered the GP contract in 2017/18, using an electronic frailty index computed from the primary care record. Both are age-restricted by design, which is why they narrow the gap without closing it.

[^crf]: Reference standards for cardiorespiratory fitness measured by cardiopulmonary exercise testing come from the FRIEND registry and are published as percentiles by age and sex: Kaminsky, Arena, Myers et al., ["Updated Reference Standards for Cardiorespiratory Fitness Measured with Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing," *Mayo Clinic Proceedings* 2022;97(2):285–293](https://www.mayoclinicproceedings.org/article/S0025-6196(21)00645-5/fulltext), [PMID 34809986](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34809986/). Ross et al., "Importance of Assessing Cardiorespiratory Fitness in Clinical Practice: A Case for Fitness as a Clinical Vital Sign," *Circulation* 2016;134:e653–e699, [PMID 27881567](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27881567/), argued for treating it as a vital sign. Note what percentiles fix and what they leave: they say where you rank, and they do not say what ranking there means for you.

[^allostatic]: Allostatic load has no settled operationalisation after three decades of use. Reviews report indices built from six to sixteen biomarkers, with no consistent method across studies and no gold standard for computation: see ["Measuring allostatic load: Approaches and limitations to algorithm creation," *Journal of Psychosomatic Research* 2022](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S002239992200335X). I cite it as support rather than as a counterexample. The one construct pointed squarely at cumulative wear is the one nobody has standardised.

[^gbd]: [The Global Burden of Disease study](https://www.healthdata.org/research-analysis/gbd) reports disability-adjusted life years, the sum of years of life lost and years lived with disability. It is the most careful health accounting anyone has built, and its unit is loss.

[^phil]: The "95% of PhDs never took a philosophy course" line is my own bet rather than a measurement, made in a January 2025 post: <https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7288609024235720704/>. The quoted sentence in that post runs to statistics rather than philosophy: *"Probably <50% took a stats course. Statistics and philosophy are tightly related, but training in either is very uncommon."*

[^piaac]: OECD, *Survey of Adult Skills 2023*, United States country note, and NCES, [Highlights of the 2023 U.S. PIAAC Results](https://nces.ed.gov/surveys/piaac/2023/national_results.asp) (NCES 2024-202). US adults averaged 249 in numeracy, below the OECD average, with 34% at or below Level 1 against an OECD average of 25%; the share at or below Level 1 rose from 29% to 34% in numeracy and from 19% to 28% in literacy between 2017 and 2023. Two caveats worth carrying: the overall response rate was 28%, and NCES itself warns that comparisons across cycles need care because the framework was revised, administration moved to tablet-only, and basic-skills items counted toward overall scores only in 2023, which mechanically moves some adults down a level. OECD reports ages 16–65 and NCES sampled 16–74, so the denominators are not interchangeable.

[^naal]: Kutner, Greenberg, Jin & Paulsen, *The Health Literacy of America's Adults: Results From the 2003 National Assessment of Adult Literacy*, NCES 2006-483, [free PDF](https://nces.ed.gov/pubs2006/2006483.pdf). The BMI-graph task is scored at 290 on the 0–500 health-literacy scale, inside the Intermediate band (226–309); 12% of adults reached Proficient and 53% Intermediate, so "beyond roughly half" is my reading of a task sitting in the upper part of the Intermediate range and not a figure the report states, which is why the body now carries the hedge too. Two things I am not doing with this source: NAAL's own category names are Below Basic, Basic, Intermediate and Proficient, and the report never calls Basic "inadequate," so the widely quoted "36% have limited health literacy" is a derived sum with an editorial gloss on top. It is also 23 years old and has never been repeated, which is its own comment on how much we wanted to know.

[^formats]: Gigerenzer, Gaissmaier, Kurz-Milcke, Schwartz & Woloshin, "Helping doctors and patients make sense of health statistics," *Psychological Science in the Public Interest* 2007;8(2):53–96, [free PDF](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/157/Papers/health_stats.pdf). The 21% and 87% come from a continuing-education session with 160 German gynecologists rather than from a survey with a sampling frame, and the question was multiple choice with four options, which is what makes 21% worse than chance. **Correction, 2026-08-06:** this essay published saying that the same facts restated as natural frequencies produced 87%, and called the result a demonstration that format carries the failure. The source reports the improvement after a training session that taught the translation into natural frequencies, so the design confounds format with teaching. The passage above has been rewritten to say only what the study can support.

[^wegwarth]: Wegwarth, Schwartz, Woloshin, Gaissmaier & Gigerenzer, "Do physicians understand cancer screening statistics? A national survey of primary care physicians in the United States," *Annals of Internal Medicine* 2012;156(5):340–349, [PMID 22393129](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22393129/). 412 physicians across two waves from a research panel; 69% recommended a test on statistically irrelevant evidence versus 23% on relevant evidence. The scenarios were hypothetical rather than observed practice, and the data are from 2010–11.

[^readability]: Rooney, Santiago, Perni, et al., "Readability of patient education materials from high-impact medical journals: a 20-year analysis," *Journal of Patient Experience* 2021;8, [PMC8205335](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8205335/). 2,585 materials, mean grade level 11.2 to 13.8 across seven metrics; 2.1% met the AMA's sixth-grade recommendation and 8.2% the NIH's eighth-grade one. Readability formulas count syllables and sentence length rather than conceptual difficulty, and journal materials are a narrow slice, so this is evidence of a mismatch rather than a measure of comprehension.
